item.title: [Agriculture 101 #4] Your Soil Is a Bank Account — Here's How the Deposits and Withdrawals Work
item.body:
> Plants need 17 essential elements, but three of them (N, P, K) do most of the heavy lifting — and soil pH quietly decides how much of any of them a root can actually reach.

## 오늘의 개념

Think of soil as a checking account that plants draw from every day.

Plants build themselves out of **essential elements** — nutrients that, if missing, mean the plant literally cannot complete its life cycle. There are 17 of them. Three come free from air and water: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen. The other 14 come from the soil.

Those 14 split into two groups by *quantity needed*, not importance:

- **Macronutrients** (needed in large amounts): nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), plus calcium, magnesium, and sulfur.
- **Micronutrients** (needed in trace amounts): iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine, nickel.

A micronutrient deficiency will kill a crop just as dead as a nitrogen shortage. The difference is how much you have to add.

**The Big Three.** Every bag of fertilizer in the U.S. carries three numbers on the front — say, `10-10-10`. That's the guaranteed analysis: percent nitrogen, percent phosphate (P₂O₅), percent potash (K₂O), by weight. A 50 lb bag of 10-10-10 contains 5 lb of N, 5 lb of phosphate, and 5 lb of potash. The rest is carrier and filler.

Roughly what each does:
- **Nitrogen** — leaves and stems, chlorophyll, protein. Deficiency shows as pale yellowing on the *oldest* leaves first, because the plant scavenges N from old tissue and moves it to new growth.
- **Phosphorus** — roots, energy transfer, flowering and seed set. Deficiency can show as dull purple-tinged leaves.
- **Potassium** — water regulation, stomatal control, disease resistance, stalk strength. Deficiency often shows as scorched leaf margins.

**Now the part most people skip: pH.**

Soil pH is a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil solution is, on a 0–14 scale where 7 is neutral. It matters because **pH controls nutrient availability**. You can have plenty of phosphorus in the soil and still starve the crop, because at low pH the phosphorus binds with iron and aluminum into forms roots can't take up. At high pH it binds with calcium instead. Phosphorus is most available roughly between pH 6.0 and 7.0 — which is why most field crops and garden vegetables are happiest in the pH 6.0–7.0 window.

Iron, manganese, and zinc run the opposite way: they get *more* available as soil turns acidic. That's why azaleas and blueberries — acid-lovers — go chlorotic and yellow in alkaline soil. They can't get iron.

**Buffering capacity** is why fixing pH is harder than it sounds. If you add acid to distilled water, the pH plunges. Add the same acid to soil and it barely moves. That resistance is buffering, and it comes from the soil's reserve of exchangeable acidity sitting on clay particles and organic matter — a large hidden pool that keeps refilling the soil solution as you neutralize it.

Practical consequence: a heavy clay soil rich in organic matter needs *far more* lime to raise its pH one unit than a sandy soil does. That's why a soil test doesn't just report pH — it reports a **buffer pH** or **lime requirement**, which is the number that actually tells you how much lime to spread.

```
Soil test pH   -> where you are now
Buffer pH      -> how hard it will be to move
Lime rate      -> tons per acre to get where you want
```

The general rules of thumb: **lime** (calcium carbonate) raises pH; **elemental sulfur** lowers it. Both work slowly — months, sometimes a full season — because they depend on soil moisture, temperature, and microbial activity.

One more piece of vocabulary that ties it together: **cation exchange capacity (CEC)**. Clay and organic matter carry negative charges, and positively charged nutrients — calcium, magnesium, potassium, ammonium — stick to those sites like magnets on a fridge. High CEC means a soil holds a large nutrient reserve and buffers strongly. Low CEC (sandy soil) means nutrients leach through fast. Same fertilizer, very different behavior.

## 일상 속에서

Say you're in Ohio and you plant tomatoes in the same backyard bed for the third summer running. You fertilize religiously with a high-nitrogen lawn-style product because it's what's in the garage. You get magnificent, dark green, four-foot vines — and almost no fruit.

That's textbook nutrient imbalance. Excess nitrogen pushes vegetative growth at the expense of flowering and fruit set. Meanwhile, three seasons of removing tomatoes has been quietly withdrawing potassium and phosphorus from the account with no matching deposit. And in much of the eastern U.S., where rainfall gradually leaches calcium and magnesium out of the topsoil, the pH has been drifting downward year over year — possibly into the mid-5s, where phosphorus availability drops sharply.

The fix costs less than a bag of fertilizer. Nearly every state has a land-grant university extension service — Ohio State, Penn State, NC State, Texas A&M — running soil testing labs, typically in the $15–$25 range per sample. You send in a composite of 10–15 cores from around the bed. What comes back is pH, buffer pH, extractable P and K, calcium, magnesium, organic matter percentage, and CEC, plus a recommendation in pounds per 1,000 square feet.

If the report says pH 5.4 with a lime requirement of 50 lb per 1,000 sq ft, spreading that lime the previous fall will do more for next year's tomatoes than any amount of fertilizer applied in June. You're not adding nutrients — you're unlocking the ones already sitting there.

There's an environmental side too. Nutrients you apply beyond what the crop can use don't vanish. Nitrate leaches into groundwater; phosphorus runs off into surface water and feeds algal blooms. The recurring summer blooms in Lake Erie and the hypoxic "dead zone" in the Gulf of Mexico are both driven substantially by nutrient runoff from a very large watershed. Matching the rate to the actual soil test is the single cheapest thing that helps both your yield and the water downstream.

The professional framing for this is the **4Rs**: Right source, Right rate, Right time, Right place. Pick the fertilizer form that fits, apply only what the test calls for, put it down when the crop can use it, and place it where roots will find it.

## 3줄 정리

1. Plants need 17 essential elements; N, P, and K are needed in the largest amounts, which is why every fertilizer bag carries three numbers (`N-P₂O₅-K₂O`) on the front.
2. Soil pH governs whether nutrients are chemically *available* to roots — phosphorus peaks around pH 6.0–7.0, while iron and zinc become more available as soil turns acidic.
3. Buffering capacity, driven by clay and organic matter, resists pH change — so a soil test's buffer pH, not the pH alone, tells you how much lime to apply.

## ✅ 셀프 퀴즈

**Q1.** A 50 lb bag of fertilizer is labeled `10-20-10`. How many pounds of actual phosphate (P₂O₅) does it contain?

- A) 5 lb
- B) 10 lb
- C) 20 lb
- D) 50 lb

**Q2.** O/X — Two soils both test at pH 5.5, so they will both need the same amount of lime to reach pH 6.5.

**Q3.** A gardener's soil has plenty of iron in it, but the plants show yellowing between the leaf veins (chlorosis). Which condition is the most likely cause?

- A) Soil pH is too low (strongly acidic)
- B) Soil pH is too high (alkaline)
- C) Nitrogen was over-applied
- D) The soil has no cation exchange capacity

## 📚 오늘의 용어

- **Essential element** — A nutrient a plant cannot complete its life cycle without, and whose role no other element can substitute for; there are 17.
- **Macronutrient / Micronutrient** — Classification by the *amount* a plant needs, not by importance; both categories are equally essential.
- **Guaranteed analysis (N-P-K)** — The three numbers on a fertilizer label giving percent nitrogen, percent phosphate (P₂O₅), and percent potash (K₂O) by weight.
- **Soil pH** — The acidity or alkalinity of the soil solution on a 0–14 scale; it determines the chemical form, and therefore the availability, of most nutrients.
- **Buffering capacity** — A soil's resistance to pH change, supplied by exchangeable acidity held on clay and organic matter; it sets how much lime or sulfur is actually required.
- **Cation exchange capacity (CEC)** — The soil's total capacity to hold positively charged nutrients on negatively charged clay and organic matter surfaces; a proxy for nutrient-holding ability.

---

*정답: **Q1 → B (10 lb).** The middle number is percent by weight, so 20% of 50 lb = 10 lb of phosphate. Note this is P₂O₅, the oxide form used on labels, not elemental phosphorus — elemental P would be about 44% of that figure.*

***Q2 → X (False).** Identical pH does not mean identical lime requirement. A heavy clay soil high in organic matter has a large reserve of exchangeable acidity — high buffering — and may need several times the lime a sandy soil needs to make the same pH move. This is exactly why soil test reports include a buffer pH.*

***Q3 → B.** Iron becomes progressively less soluble as pH rises; in alkaline soil it precipitates into forms roots cannot absorb. The plant is iron-deficient despite iron being physically present — a good illustration that total nutrient content and plant-available nutrient content are two different things. Interveinal chlorosis on the youngest leaves is the classic symptom, because iron is not readily remobilized within the plant.*
